5	# Create custom subagents
6	
7	> Create and use specialized AI subagents in Claude Code for task-specific workflows and improved context management.
8	
9	Subagents are specialized AI assistants that handle specific types of tasks. Use one when a side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again: the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary. Define a custom subagent when you keep spawning the same kind of worker with the same instructions.
10	
11	Each subagent runs in its own context window with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions. When Claude encounters a task that matches a subagent's description, it delegates to that subagent, which works independently and returns results. To see the context savings in practice, the [context window visualization](/en/context-window) walks through a session where a subagent handles research in its own separate window.
12	
13	<Note>
14	  Subagents work within a single session. To run many independent sessions in parallel and monitor them from one place, see [background agents](/en/agent-view). For sessions that communicate with each other, see [agent teams](/en/agent-teams).
15	</Note>
16	
17	Subagents help you:
18	
19	* **Preserve context** by keeping exploration and implementation out of your main conversation
20	* **Enforce constraints** by limiting which tools a subagent can use
21	* **Reuse configurations** across projects with user-level subagents
22	* **Specialize behavior** with focused system prompts for specific domains
23	* **Control costs** by routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku
24	
25	Claude uses each subagent's description to decide when to delegate tasks. When you create a subagent, write a clear description so Claude knows when to use it.
26	
27	Claude Code includes several built-in subagents like **Explore**, **Plan**, and **general-purpose**. You can also create custom subagents to handle specific tasks. This page covers:
28	
29	* [Built-in subagents](#built-in-subagents)
30	* [How to create your own](#quickstart-create-your-first-subagent)
31	* [Full configuration options](#configure-subagents)
32	* [Patterns for working with subagents](#work-with-subagents)
33	* [Forked subagents](#fork-the-current-conversation)
34	* [Example subagents](#example-subagents)
35	
36	## Built-in subagents
37	
38	Claude Code includes built-in subagents that Claude automatically uses when appropriate. Each inherits the parent conversation's permissions with additional tool restrictions.
39	
40	Explore and Plan skip your CLAUDE.md files and the parent session's git status to keep research fast and inexpensive. Every other built-in and [custom subagent](#configure-subagents) loads both. For the full breakdown of what reaches a subagent, see [what loads at startup](#what-loads-at-startup).
41	
42	<Tabs>
43	  <Tab title="Explore">
44	    A fast, read-only agent optimized for searching and analyzing codebases.
45	
46	    * **Model**: Haiku (fast, low-latency)
47	    * **Tools**: Read-only tools (denied access to Write and Edit tools)
48	    * **Purpose**: File discovery, code search, codebase exploration
49	
50	    Claude delegates to Explore when it needs to search or understand a codebase without making changes. This keeps exploration results out of your main conversation context.
51	
52	    When invoking Explore, Claude specifies a thoroughness level: **quick** for targeted lookups, **medium** for balanced exploration, or **very thorough** for comprehensive analysis.
53	  </Tab>
54	
55	  <Tab title="Plan">
56	    A research agent used during [plan mode](/en/permission-modes#analyze-before-you-edit-with-plan-mode) to gather context before presenting a plan.
57	
58	    * **Model**: Inherits from main conversation
59	    * **Tools**: Read-only tools (denied access to Write and Edit tools)
60	    * **Purpose**: Codebase research for planning
61	
62	    When you're in plan mode and Claude needs to understand your codebase, it delegates research to the Plan subagent. This prevents infinite nesting (subagents cannot spawn other subagents) while still gathering necessary context.
63	  </Tab>
64	
65	  <Tab title="General-purpose">
66	    A capable agent for complex, multi-step tasks that require both exploration and action.
67	
68	    * **Model**: Inherits from main conversation
69	    * **Tools**: All tools
70	    * **Purpose**: Complex research, multi-step operations, code modifications
71	
72	    Claude delegates to general-purpose when the task requires both exploration and modification, complex reasoning to interpret results, or multiple dependent steps.
73	  </Tab>
74	
75	  <Tab title="Other">
76	    Claude Code includes additional helper agents for specific tasks. These are typically invoked automatically, so you don't need to use them directly.
77	
78	    | Agent             | Model  | When Claude uses it                                      |
79	    | :---------------- | :----- | :------------------------------------------------------- |
80	    | statusline-setup  | Sonnet | When you run `/statusline` to configure your status line |
81	    | claude-code-guide | Haiku  | When you ask questions about Claude Code features        |
82	  </Tab>
83	</Tabs>
84	
85	Built-in subagents are always registered in interactive sessions. To block a specific built-in type, add it to `permissions.deny` as shown in [Disable specific subagents](#disable-specific-subagents). To prevent Claude from delegating to any subagent, deny the `Agent` tool itself with [`permissions.deny`](/en/permissions#tool-specific-permission-rules). In [non-interactive mode](/en/headless) and the [Agent SDK](/en/agent-sdk/overview), set [`CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1`](/en/env-vars) to remove all built-in types and supply only your own.
86	
87	Beyond these built-in subagents, you can create your own with custom prompts, tool restrictions, permission modes, hooks, and skills. The following sections show how to get started and customize subagents.
88	
89	## Quickstart: create your first subagent
90	
91	Subagents are defined in Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. You can [create them manually](#write-subagent-files) or use the `/agents` command.
92	
93	This walkthrough guides you through creating a user-level subagent with the `/agents` command. The subagent reviews code and suggests improvements for the codebase.
94	
95	<Steps>
96	  <Step title="Open the subagents interface">
97	    In Claude Code, run:
98	
99	    ```text theme={null}
100	    /agents
101	    ```
102	  </Step>
103	
104	  <Step title="Choose a location">
105	    Switch to the **Library** tab, select **Create new agent**, then choose **Personal**. This saves the subagent to `~/.claude/agents/` so it's available in all your projects.
106	  </Step>
107	
108	  <Step title="Generate with Claude">
109	    Select **Generate with Claude**. When prompted, describe the subagent:
110	
111	    ```text theme={null}
112	    A code improvement agent that scans files and suggests improvements
113	    for readability, performance, and best practices. It should explain
114	    each issue, show the current code, and provide an improved version.
115	    ```
116	
117	    Claude generates the identifier, description, and system prompt for you.
118	  </Step>
119	
120	  <Step title="Select tools">
121	    For a read-only reviewer, deselect everything except **Read-only tools**. If you keep all tools selected, the subagent inherits all tools available to the main conversation.
122	  </Step>
123	
124	  <Step title="Select model">
125	    Choose which model the subagent uses. For this example agent, select **Sonnet**, which balances capability and speed for analyzing code patterns.
126	  </Step>
127	
128	  <Step title="Choose a color">
129	    Pick a background color for the subagent. This helps you identify which subagent is running in the UI.
130	  </Step>
131	
132	  <Step title="Configure memory">
133	    Select **User scope** to give the subagent a [persistent memory directory](#enable-persistent-memory) at `~/.claude/agent-memory/`. The subagent uses this to accumulate insights across conversations, such as codebase patterns and recurring issues. Select **None** if you don't want the subagent to persist learnings.
134	  </Step>
135	
136	  <Step title="Save and try it out">
137	    Review the configuration summary. Press `s` or `Enter` to save, or press `e` to save and edit the file in your editor. The subagent is available immediately. Try it:
138	
139	    ```text theme={null}
140	    Use the code-improver agent to suggest improvements in this project
141	    ```
142	
143	    Claude delegates to your new subagent, which scans the codebase and returns improvement suggestions.
144	  </Step>
145	</Steps>
146	
147	You now have a subagent you can use in any project on your machine to analyze codebases and suggest improvements.
148	
149	You can also create subagents manually as Markdown files, define them via CLI flags, or distribute them through plugins. The following sections cover all configuration options.
150	
151	## Configure subagents
152	
153	### Use the /agents command
154	
155	The `/agents` command opens a tabbed interface for managing subagents. The **Running** tab shows live subagents and lets you open or stop them. The **Library** tab lets you:
156	
157	* View all available subagents (built-in, user, project, and plugin)
158	* Create new subagents with guided setup or Claude generation
159	* Edit existing subagent configuration and tool access
160	* Delete custom subagents
161	* See which subagents are active when duplicates exist
162	
163	This is the recommended way to create and manage subagents. For manual creation or automation, you can also add subagent files directly.
164	
165	### Choose the subagent scope
166	
167	Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. Store them in different locations depending on scope. When multiple subagents share the same name, the higher-priority location wins.
168	
169	| Location                     | Scope                   | Priority    | How to create                                 |
170	| :--------------------------- | :---------------------- | :---------- | :-------------------------------------------- |
171	| Managed settings             | Organization-wide       | 1 (highest) | Deployed via [managed settings](/en/settings) |
172	| `--agents` CLI flag          | Current session         | 2           | Pass JSON when launching Claude Code          |
173	| `.claude/agents/`            | Current project         | 3           | Interactive or manual                         |
174	| `~/.claude/agents/`          | All your projects       | 4           | Interactive or manual                         |
175	| Plugin's `agents/` directory | Where plugin is enabled | 5 (lowest)  | Installed with [plugins](/en/plugins)         |
176	
177	**Project subagents** (`.claude/agents/`) are ideal for subagents specific to a codebase. Check them into version control so your team can use and improve them collaboratively.
178	
179	Project subagents are discovered by walking up from the current working directory. Directories added with `--add-dir` [grant file access only](/en/permissions#additional-directories-grant-file-access-not-configuration) and are not scanned for subagents. To share subagents across projects, use `~/.claude/agents/` or a [plugin](/en/plugins).
180	
181	**User subagents** (`~/.claude/agents/`) are personal subagents available in all your projects.
182	
183	Claude Code scans `.claude/agents/` and `~/.claude/agents/` recursively, so you can organize definitions into subfolders such as `agents/review/` or `agents/research/`. The subdirectory path does not affect how a subagent is identified or invoked, because identity comes only from the `name` frontmatter field. Keep `name` values unique across the whole tree: if two files within one scope declare the same name, Claude Code keeps one and discards the other without warning.
184	
185	Plugin `agents/` directories are also scanned recursively. Unlike project and user scopes, a subfolder inside a plugin's `agents/` directory becomes part of the [scoped identifier](#invoke-subagents-explicitly): a file at `agents/review/security.md` in plugin `my-plugin` registers as `my-plugin:review:security`.
186	
187	**CLI-defined subagents** are passed as JSON when launching Claude Code. They exist only for that session and aren't saved to disk, making them useful for quick testing or automation scripts. You can define multiple subagents in a single `--agents` call:
188	
189	<Tabs>
190	  <Tab title="macOS, Linux, WSL">
191	    ```bash theme={null}
192	    claude --agents '{
193	      "code-reviewer": {
194	        "description": "Expert code reviewer. Use proactively after code changes.",
195	        "prompt": "You are a senior code reviewer. Focus on code quality, security, and best practices.",
196	        "tools": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash"],
197	        "model": "sonnet"
198	      },
199	      "debugger": {
200	        "description": "Debugging specialist for errors and test failures.",
201	        "prompt": "You are an expert debugger. Analyze errors, identify root causes, and provide fixes."
202	      }
203	    }'
204	    ```
205	  </Tab>
206	
207	  <Tab title="Windows PowerShell">
208	    ```powershell theme={null}
209	    claude --agents @'
210	    {
211	      "code-reviewer": {
212	        "description": "Expert code reviewer. Use proactively after code changes.",
213	        "prompt": "You are a senior code reviewer. Focus on code quality, security, and best practices.",
214	        "tools": ["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Bash"],
215	        "model": "sonnet"
216	      },
217	      "debugger": {
218	        "description": "Debugging specialist for errors and test failures.",
219	        "prompt": "You are an expert debugger. Analyze errors, identify root causes, and provide fixes."
220	      }
221	    }
222	    '@
223	    ```
224	  </Tab>
225	</Tabs>
226	
227	The `--agents` flag accepts JSON with the same [frontmatter](#supported-frontmatter-fields) fields as file-based subagents: `description`, `prompt`, `tools`, `disallowedTools`, `model`, `permissionMode`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `initialPrompt`, `memory`, `effort`, `background`, `isolation`, and `color`. Use `prompt` for the system prompt, equivalent to the markdown body in file-based subagents.
228	
229	**Managed subagents** are deployed by organization administrators. Place markdown files in `.claude/agents/` inside the [managed settings directory](/en/settings#settings-files), using the same frontmatter format as project and user subagents. Managed definitions take precedence over project and user subagents with the same name.
230	
231	**Plugin subagents** come from [plugins](/en/plugins) you've installed. They appear in `/agents` alongside your custom subagents. See the [plugin components reference](/en/plugins-reference#agents) for details on creating plugin subagents.
232	
233	<Note>
234	  For security reasons, plugin subagents do not support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields. These fields are ignored when loading agents from a plugin. If you need them, copy the agent file into `.claude/agents/` or `~/.claude/agents/`. You can also add rules to [`permissions.allow`](/en/settings#permission-settings) in `settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, but these rules apply to the entire session, not just the plugin subagent.
235	</Note>
236	
237	Subagent definitions from any of these scopes are also available to [agent teams](/en/agent-teams#use-subagent-definitions-for-teammates): when spawning a teammate, you can reference a subagent type and the teammate uses its `tools` and `model`, with the definition's body appended to the teammate's system prompt as additional instructions. See [agent teams](/en/agent-teams#use-subagent-definitions-for-teammates) for which frontmatter fields apply on that path.
238	
239	### Write subagent files
240	
241	Subagent files use YAML frontmatter for configuration, followed by the system prompt in Markdown:
242	
243	<Note>
244	  Subagents are loaded at session start. If you add or edit a subagent file directly on disk, restart your session to load it. Subagents created through the `/agents` interface take effect immediately without a restart.
245	</Note>
246	
247	```markdown theme={null}
248	---
249	name: code-reviewer
250	description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
251	tools: Read, Glob, Grep
252	model: sonnet
253	---
254	
255	You are a code reviewer. When invoked, analyze the code and provide
256	specific, actionable feedback on quality, security, and best practices.
257	```
258	
259	The frontmatter defines the subagent's metadata and configuration. The body becomes the system prompt that guides the subagent's behavior. Subagents receive only this system prompt (plus basic environment details like working directory), not the full Claude Code system prompt.
260	
261	A subagent starts in the main conversation's current working directory. Within a subagent, `cd` commands do not persist between Bash or PowerShell tool calls and do not affect the main conversation's working directory. To give the subagent an isolated copy of the repository instead, set [`isolation: worktree`](#supported-frontmatter-fields).
262	
263	#### Supported frontmatter fields
264	
265	The following fields can be used in the YAML frontmatter. Only `name` and `description` are required.
266	
267	| Field             | Required | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
268	| :---------------- | :------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
269	| `name`            | Yes      | Unique identifier using lowercase letters and hyphens. [Hooks](/en/hooks#subagentstart) receive this value as `agent_type`. The filename does not have to match                                                                                                                                                                          |
270	| `description`     | Yes      | When Claude should delegate to this subagent                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
271	| `tools`           | No       | [Tools](#available-tools) the subagent can use. Inherits all tools if omitted. To preload Skills into context, use the `skills` field rather than listing `Skill` here                                                                                                                                                                   |
272	| `disallowedTools` | No       | Tools to deny, removed from inherited or specified list                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
273	| `model`           | No       | [Model](#choose-a-model) to use: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full model ID (for example, `claude-opus-4-8`), or `inherit`. Defaults to `inherit`                                                                                                                                                                               |
274	| `permissionMode`  | No       | [Permission mode](#permission-modes): `default`, `acceptEdits`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`, or `plan`. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope)                                                                                                                                                            |
275	| `maxTurns`        | No       | Maximum number of agentic turns before the subagent stops                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
276	| `skills`          | No       | [Skills](/en/skills) to preload into the subagent's context at startup. The full skill content is injected, not just the description. Subagents can still invoke unlisted project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool                                                                                                        |
277	| `mcpServers`      | No       | [MCP servers](/en/mcp) available to this subagent. Each entry is either a server name referencing an already-configured server (e.g., `"slack"`) or an inline definition with the server name as key and a full [MCP server config](/en/mcp#installing-mcp-servers) as value. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope) |
278	| `hooks`           | No       | [Lifecycle hooks](#define-hooks-for-subagents) scoped to this subagent. Ignored for [plugin subagents](#choose-the-subagent-scope)                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
279	| `memory`          | No       | [Persistent memory scope](#enable-persistent-memory): `user`, `project`, or `local`. Enables cross-session learning                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
280	| `background`      | No       | Set to `true` to always run this subagent as a [background task](#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background). Default: `false`                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
281	| `effort`          | No       | Effort level when this subagent is active. Overrides the session effort level. Default: inherits from session. Options: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`; available levels depend on the model                                                                                                                                    |
282	| `isolation`       | No       | Set to `worktree` to run the subagent in a temporary [git worktree](/en/worktrees), giving it an isolated copy of the repository branched by default from your [default branch](/en/worktrees#choose-the-base-branch) rather than the parent session's `HEAD`. The worktree is automatically cleaned up if the subagent makes no changes |
283	| `color`           | No       | Display color for the subagent in the task list and transcript. Accepts `red`, `blue`, `green`, `yellow`, `purple`, `orange`, `pink`, or `cyan`                                                                                                                                                                                          |
284	| `initialPrompt`   | No       | Auto-submitted as the first user turn when this agent runs as the main session agent (via `--agent` or the `agent` setting). [Commands](/en/commands) and [skills](/en/skills) are processed. Prepended to any user-provided prompt                                                                                                      |
285	
286	### Choose a model
287	
288	The `model` field controls which [AI model](/en/model-config) the subagent uses:
289	
290	* **Model alias**: Use one of the available aliases: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, or `fable`
291	* **Full model ID**: Use a full model ID such as `claude-opus-4-8` or `claude-sonnet-4-6`. Accepts the same values as the `--model` flag
292	* **inherit**: Use the same model as the main conversation
293	* **Omitted**: If not specified, defaults to `inherit` (uses the same model as the main conversation)
294	
295	When Claude invokes a subagent, it can also pass a `model` parameter for that specific invocation. Claude Code resolves the subagent's model in this order:
296	
297	1. The [`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`](/en/model-config#environment-variables) environment variable, if set
298	2. The per-invocation `model` parameter
299	3. The subagent definition's `model` frontmatter
300	4. The main conversation's model
301	
302	### Control subagent capabilities
303	
304	You can control what subagents can do through tool access, permission modes, and conditional rules.
305	
306	#### Available tools
307	
308	Subagents inherit the [internal tools](/en/tools-reference) and MCP tools available in the main conversation by default. The following tools depend on the main conversation's UI or session state and are not available to subagents, even when listed in the `tools` field:
309	
310	* `Agent`
311	* `AskUserQuestion`
312	* `EnterPlanMode`
313	* `ExitPlanMode`, unless the subagent's [`permissionMode`](#permission-modes) is `plan`
314	* `ScheduleWakeup`
315	* `WaitForMcpServers`
316	
317	To restrict tools, use either the `tools` field (allowlist) or the `disallowedTools` field (denylist). This example uses `tools` to exclusively allow Read, Grep, Glob, and Bash. The subagent can't edit files, write files, or use any MCP tools:
318	
319	```yaml theme={null}
320	---
321	name: safe-researcher
322	description: Research agent with restricted capabilities
323	tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
324	---
325	```
326	
327	This example uses `disallowedTools` to inherit every tool from the main conversation except Write and Edit. The subagent keeps Bash, MCP tools, and everything else:
328	
329	```yaml theme={null}
330	---
331	name: no-writes
332	description: Inherits every tool except file writes
333	disallowedTools: Write, Edit
334	---
335	```
336	
337	If both are set, `disallowedTools` is applied first, then `tools` is resolved against the remaining pool. A tool listed in both is removed.
338	
339	#### Restrict which subagents can be spawned
340	
341	When an agent runs as the main thread with `claude --agent`, it can spawn subagents using the Agent tool. To restrict which subagent types it can spawn, use `Agent(agent_type)` syntax in the `tools` field.
342	
343	<Note>In version 2.1.63, the Task tool was renamed to Agent. Existing `Task(...)` references in settings and agent definitions still work as aliases.</Note>
344	
345	```yaml theme={null}
346	---
347	name: coordinator
348	description: Coordinates work across specialized agents
349	tools: Agent(worker, researcher), Read, Bash
350	---
351	```
352	
353	This is an allowlist: only the `worker` and `researcher` subagents can be spawned. If the agent tries to spawn any other type, the request fails and the agent sees only the allowed types in its prompt. To block specific agents while allowing all others, use [`permissions.deny`](#disable-specific-subagents) instead.
354	
355	To allow spawning any subagent without restrictions, use `Agent` without parentheses:
356	
357	```yaml theme={null}
358	tools: Agent, Read, Bash
359	```
360	
361	If `Agent` is omitted from the `tools` list entirely, the agent cannot spawn any subagents. This restriction only applies to agents running as the main thread with `claude --agent`. Subagents cannot spawn other subagents, so `Agent(agent_type)` has no effect in subagent definitions.
362	
363	#### Scope MCP servers to a subagent
364	
365	Use the `mcpServers` field to give a subagent access to [MCP](/en/mcp) servers that aren't available in the main conversation. Inline servers defined here are connected when the subagent starts and disconnected when it finishes. String references share the parent session's connection.
366	
367	<Note>
368	  The `mcpServers` field applies in both contexts where an agent file can run:
369	
370	  * As a subagent, spawned through the Agent tool or an @-mention
371	  * As the main session, launched with [`--agent`](#invoke-subagents-explicitly) or the `agent` setting
372	
373	  When the agent is the main session, inline server definitions connect at startup alongside servers from [`.mcp.json`](/en/mcp) and settings files.
374	</Note>
375	
376	Each entry in the list is either an inline server definition or a string referencing an MCP server already configured in your session:
377	
378	```yaml theme={null}
379	---
380	name: browser-tester
381	description: Tests features in a real browser using Playwright
382	mcpServers:
383	  # Inline definition: scoped to this subagent only
384	  - playwright:
385	      type: stdio
386	      command: npx
387	      args: ["-y", "@playwright/mcp@latest"]
388	  # Reference by name: reuses an already-configured server
389	  - github
390	---
391	
392	Use the Playwright tools to navigate, screenshot, and interact with pages.

395	Inline definitions use the same schema as `.mcp.json` server entries (`stdio`, `http`, `sse`, `ws`), keyed by the server name.
396	
397	To keep an MCP server out of the main conversation entirely and avoid its tool descriptions consuming context there, define it inline here rather than in `.mcp.json`. The subagent gets the tools; the parent conversation does not.

399	As of v2.1.153, the MCP restrictions that apply to the main session also cover servers declared in subagent frontmatter:
400	
401	* [`--strict-mcp-config`](/en/cli-reference) and [`--bare`](/en/cli-reference)
402	* [Enterprise managed MCP configuration](/en/managed-mcp)

409	#### Permission modes
410	
411	The `permissionMode` field controls how the subagent handles permission prompts. Subagents inherit the permission context from the main conversation and can override the mode, except when the parent mode takes precedence as described below.
412	
413	| Mode                | Behavior                                                                                                                                    |
414	| :------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
415	| `default`           | Standard permission checking with prompts                                                                                                   |
416	| `acceptEdits`       | Auto-accept file edits and common filesystem commands for paths in the working directory or `additionalDirectories`                         |
417	| `auto`              | [Auto mode](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode): a background classifier reviews commands and protected-directory writes |
418	| `dontAsk`           | Auto-deny permission prompts (explicitly allowed tools still work)                                                                          |
419	| `bypassPermissions` | Skip permission prompts                                                                                                                     |
420	| `plan`              | Plan mode (read-only exploration)                                                                                                           |
421	
422	<Warning>
423	  Use `bypassPermissions` with caution. It skips permission prompts, allowing the subagent to execute operations without approval, including writes to `.git`, `.config/git`, `.claude`, `.vscode`, `.idea`, `.husky`, `.cargo`, `.devcontainer`, `.yarn`, and `.mvn`. Explicit [`ask` rules](/en/permissions#manage-permissions) and root and home directory removals such as `rm -rf /` still prompt. See [permission modes](/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) for details.
424	</Warning>
425	
426	If the parent uses `bypassPermissions` or `acceptEdits`, this takes precedence and cannot be overridden. If the parent uses [auto mode](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode), the subagent inherits auto mode and any `permissionMode` in its frontmatter is ignored: the classifier evaluates the subagent's tool calls with the same block and allow rules as the parent session.
427	
428	#### Preload skills into subagents
429	
430	Use the `skills` field to inject skill content into a subagent's context at startup. This gives the subagent domain knowledge without requiring it to discover and load skills during execution.
431	
432	```yaml theme={null}
433	---
434	name: api-developer
435	description: Implement API endpoints following team conventions
436	skills:
437	  - api-conventions
438	  - error-handling-patterns
439	---
440	
441	Implement API endpoints. Follow the conventions and patterns from the preloaded skills.
442	```
443	
444	The full content of each listed skill is injected into the subagent's context at startup. This field controls which skills are preloaded, not which skills the subagent can access: without it, the subagent can still discover and invoke project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool during execution. To prevent a subagent from invoking skills entirely, omit `Skill` from the [`tools`](#available-tools) list or add it to `disallowedTools`.
445	
446	You cannot preload skills that set [`disable-model-invocation: true`](/en/skills#control-who-invokes-a-skill), since preloading draws from the same set of skills Claude can invoke. If a listed skill is missing or disabled, Claude Code skips it and logs a warning to the debug log.
447	
448	<Note>
449	  This is the inverse of [running a skill in a subagent](/en/skills#run-skills-in-a-subagent). With `skills` in a subagent, the subagent controls the system prompt and loads skill content. With `context: fork` in a skill, the skill content is injected into the agent you specify. Both use the same underlying system.
450	</Note>

452	#### Enable persistent memory
453	
454	The `memory` field gives the subagent a persistent directory that survives across conversations. The subagent uses this directory to build up knowledge over time, such as codebase patterns, debugging insights, and architectural decisions.
455	
456	```yaml theme={null}
457	---
458	name: code-reviewer
459	description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
460	memory: user
461	---
462	
463	You are a code reviewer. As you review code, update your agent memory with
464	patterns, conventions, and recurring issues you discover.
465	```
466	
467	Choose a scope based on how broadly the memory should apply:
468	
469	| Scope     | Location                                      | Use when                                                                                    |
470	| :-------- | :-------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
471	| `user`    | `~/.claude/agent-memory/<name-of-agent>/`     | the subagent should remember learnings across all projects                                  |
472	| `project` | `.claude/agent-memory/<name-of-agent>/`       | the subagent's knowledge is project-specific and shareable via version control              |
473	| `local`   | `.claude/agent-memory-local/<name-of-agent>/` | the subagent's knowledge is project-specific but should not be checked into version control |
474	
475	When memory is enabled:
476	
477	* The subagent's system prompt includes instructions for reading and writing to the memory directory.
478	* The subagent's system prompt also includes the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md` in the memory directory, whichever comes first, with instructions to curate `MEMORY.md` if it exceeds that limit.
479	* Read, Write, and Edit tools are automatically enabled so the subagent can manage its memory files.
480	
481	##### Persistent memory tips
482	
483	* `project` is the recommended default scope. It makes subagent knowledge shareable via version control. Use `user` when the subagent's knowledge is broadly applicable across projects, or `local` when the knowledge should not be checked into version control.
484	* Ask the subagent to consult its memory before starting work: "Review this PR, and check your memory for patterns you've seen before."
485	* Ask the subagent to update its memory after completing a task: "Now that you're done, save what you learned to your memory." Over time, this builds a knowledge base that makes the subagent more effective.
486	* Include memory instructions directly in the subagent's markdown file so it proactively maintains its own knowledge base:
487	
488	  ```markdown theme={null}
489	  Update your agent memory as you discover codepaths, patterns, library
490	  locations, and key architectural decisions. This builds up institutional
491	  knowledge across conversations. Write concise notes about what you found
492	  and where.
493	  ```

495	#### Conditional rules with hooks
496	
497	For more dynamic control over tool usage, use `PreToolUse` hooks to validate operations before they execute. This is useful when you need to allow some operations of a tool while blocking others.
498	
499	This example creates a subagent that only allows read-only database queries. The `PreToolUse` hook runs the script specified in `command` before each Bash command executes:
500	
501	```yaml theme={null}
502	---
503	name: db-reader
504	description: Execute read-only database queries
505	tools: Bash
506	hooks:
507	  PreToolUse:
508	    - matcher: "Bash"
509	      hooks:
510	        - type: command
511	          command: "./scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh"
512	---
513	```
514	
515	Claude Code [passes hook input as JSON](/en/hooks#pretooluse-input) via stdin to hook commands. The validation script reads this JSON, extracts the Bash command, and [exits with code 2](/en/hooks#exit-code-2-behavior-per-event) to block write operations:
516	
517	```bash theme={null}
518	#!/bin/bash
519	# ./scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh
520	
521	INPUT=$(cat)
522	COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')
523	
524	# Block SQL write operations (case-insensitive)
525	if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -iE '\b(INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|CREATE|ALTER|TRUNCATE)\b' > /dev/null; then
526	  echo "Blocked: Only SELECT queries are allowed" >&2
527	  exit 2
528	fi
529	
530	exit 0
531	```
532	
533	See [Hook input](/en/hooks#pretooluse-input) for the complete input schema and [exit codes](/en/hooks#exit-code-output) for how exit codes affect behavior. On Windows, write hook scripts in PowerShell and add `shell: powershell` to the hook entry as shown in [running hooks in PowerShell](/en/hooks#windows-powershell-tool).
534	
535	#### Disable specific subagents
536	
537	You can prevent Claude from using specific subagents by adding them to the `deny` array in your [settings](/en/settings#permission-settings). Use the format `Agent(subagent-name)` where `subagent-name` matches the subagent's name field.
538	
539	```json theme={null}
540	{
541	  "permissions": {
542	    "deny": ["Agent(Explore)", "Agent(my-custom-agent)"]
543	  }
544	}
545	```
546	
547	This works for both built-in and custom subagents. You can also use the `--disallowedTools` CLI flag:
548	
549	```bash theme={null}
550	claude --disallowedTools "Agent(Explore)"
551	```
552	
553	See [Permissions documentation](/en/permissions#tool-specific-permission-rules) for more details on permission rules.

555	### Define hooks for subagents
556	
557	Subagents can define [hooks](/en/hooks) that run during the subagent's lifecycle. There are two ways to configure hooks:
558	
559	1. **In the subagent's frontmatter**: Define hooks that run only while that subagent is active
560	2. **In `settings.json`**: Define hooks that run in the main session when subagents start or stop
561	
562	#### Hooks in subagent frontmatter
563	
564	Define hooks directly in the subagent's markdown file. These hooks only run while that specific subagent is active and are cleaned up when it finishes.
565	
566	<Note>
567	  Frontmatter hooks fire when the agent is spawned as a subagent through the Agent tool or an @-mention, and when the agent runs as the main session via [`--agent`](#invoke-subagents-explicitly) or the `agent` setting. In the main-session case they run alongside any hooks defined in [`settings.json`](/en/hooks).
568	</Note>
569	
570	All [hook events](/en/hooks#hook-events) are supported. The most common events for subagents are:
571	
572	| Event         | Matcher input | When it fires                                                       |
573	| :------------ | :------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------ |
574	| `PreToolUse`  | Tool name     | Before the subagent uses a tool                                     |
575	| `PostToolUse` | Tool name     | After the subagent uses a tool                                      |
576	| `Stop`        | (none)        | When the subagent finishes (converted to `SubagentStop` at runtime) |
577	
578	This example validates Bash commands with the `PreToolUse` hook and runs a linter after file edits with `PostToolUse`:
579	
580	```yaml theme={null}
581	---
582	name: code-reviewer
583	description: Review code changes with automatic linting
584	hooks:
585	  PreToolUse:
586	    - matcher: "Bash"
587	      hooks:
588	        - type: command
589	          command: "./scripts/validate-command.sh $TOOL_INPUT"
590	  PostToolUse:
591	    - matcher: "Edit|Write"
592	      hooks:
593	        - type: command
594	          command: "./scripts/run-linter.sh"
595	---
596	```
597	
598	When the agent is invoked as a subagent, `Stop` hooks in frontmatter are automatically converted to `SubagentStop` events.
599	
600	#### Project-level hooks for subagent events
601	
602	Configure hooks in `settings.json` that respond to subagent lifecycle events in the main session.
603	
604	| Event           | Matcher input   | When it fires                    |
605	| :-------------- | :-------------- | :------------------------------- |
606	| `SubagentStart` | Agent type name | When a subagent begins execution |
607	| `SubagentStop`  | Agent type name | When a subagent completes        |
608	
609	Both events support matchers to target specific agent types by name. This example runs a setup script only when the `db-agent` subagent starts, and a cleanup script when any subagent stops:
610	
611	```json theme={null}
612	{
613	  "hooks": {
614	    "SubagentStart": [
615	      {
616	        "matcher": "db-agent",
617	        "hooks": [
618	          { "type": "command", "command": "./scripts/setup-db-connection.sh" }
619	        ]
620	      }
621	    ],
622	    "SubagentStop": [
623	      {
624	        "hooks": [
625	          { "type": "command", "command": "./scripts/cleanup-db-connection.sh" }
626	        ]
627	      }
628	    ]
629	  }
630	}
631	```
632	
633	See [Hooks](/en/hooks) for the complete hook configuration format.

635	## Work with subagents
636	
637	### Understand automatic delegation
638	
639	Claude automatically delegates tasks based on the task description in your request, the `description` field in subagent configurations, and current context. To encourage proactive delegation, include phrases like "use proactively" in your subagent's description field.
640	
641	### Invoke subagents explicitly
642	
643	When automatic delegation isn't enough, you can request a subagent yourself. Three patterns escalate from a one-off suggestion to a session-wide default:
644	
645	* **Natural language**: name the subagent in your prompt; Claude decides whether to delegate
646	* **@-mention**: guarantees the subagent runs for one task
647	* **Session-wide**: the whole session uses that subagent's system prompt, tool restrictions, and model via the `--agent` flag or the `agent` setting
648	
649	For natural language, there's no special syntax. Name the subagent and Claude typically delegates:
650	
651	```text theme={null}
652	Use the test-runner subagent to fix failing tests
653	Have the code-reviewer subagent look at my recent changes
654	```
655	
656	**@-mention the subagent.** Type `@` and pick the subagent from the typeahead, the same way you @-mention files. This ensures that specific subagent runs rather than leaving the choice to Claude:
657	
658	```text theme={null}
659	@"code-reviewer (agent)" look at the auth changes
660	```
661	
662	Your full message still goes to Claude, which writes the subagent's task prompt based on what you asked. The @-mention controls which subagent Claude invokes, not what prompt it receives.
663	
664	Subagents provided by an enabled [plugin](/en/plugins) appear in the typeahead under their scoped name, such as `my-plugin:code-reviewer` or `my-plugin:review:security` when the plugin [organizes agents into subfolders](#choose-the-subagent-scope). Named background subagents currently running in the session also appear in the typeahead, showing their status next to the name. You can also type the mention manually without using the picker: `@agent-<name>` for local subagents, or `@agent-` followed by the scoped name for plugin subagents, for example `@agent-my-plugin:code-reviewer`.
665	
666	**Run the whole session as a subagent.** Pass [`--agent <name>`](/en/cli-reference) to start a session where the main thread itself takes on that subagent's system prompt, tool restrictions, and model:
667	
668	```bash theme={null}
669	claude --agent code-reviewer
670	```
671	
672	The subagent's system prompt replaces the default Claude Code system prompt entirely, the same way [`--system-prompt`](/en/cli-reference) does. `CLAUDE.md` files and project memory still load through the normal message flow. The agent name appears as `@<name>` in the startup header so you can confirm it's active.
673	
674	This works with built-in and custom subagents, and the choice persists when you resume the session.
675	
676	For a plugin-provided subagent, you can pass just the agent name and Claude Code will find it:
677	
678	```bash theme={null}
679	claude --agent security-reviewer
680	```
681	
682	If multiple plugins provide agents with the same name, pass the scoped name to disambiguate:
683	
684	```bash theme={null}
685	claude --agent my-plugin:security-reviewer
686	```
687	
688	If the plugin places the agent in a subfolder of its `agents/` directory, include the subfolder in the scoped name, for example `claude --agent my-plugin:review:security`.
689	
690	To make it the default for every session in a project, set `agent` in `.claude/settings.json`:
691	
692	```json theme={null}
693	{
694	  "agent": "code-reviewer"
695	}
696	```
697	
698	The CLI flag overrides the setting if both are present.
699	
700	### Run subagents in foreground or background
701	
702	Subagents can run in the foreground (blocking) or background (concurrent):
703	
704	* **Foreground subagents** block the main conversation until complete. Permission prompts are passed through to you as they come up.
705	* **Background subagents** run concurrently while you continue working. They run with the permissions already granted in the session and auto-deny any tool call that would otherwise prompt. If a background subagent needs to ask clarifying questions, that tool call fails but the subagent continues.
706	
707	If a background subagent fails due to missing permissions, you can start a new foreground subagent with the same task to retry with interactive prompts.
708	
709	Claude decides whether to run subagents in the foreground or background based on the task. You can also:
710	
711	* Ask Claude to "run this in the background"
712	* Press **Ctrl+B** to background a running task
713	
714	To disable all background task functionality, set the `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS` environment variable to `1`. See [Environment variables](/en/env-vars).
715	
716	When [`CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT`](#fork-the-current-conversation) is set to `1`, every subagent spawn runs in the background regardless of the `background` field. Forks still surface permission prompts in your terminal as they occur; named subagents auto-deny anything that would prompt, as described above.
717	
718	### Common patterns
719	
720	#### Isolate high-volume operations
721	
722	One of the most effective uses for subagents is isolating operations that produce large amounts of output. Running tests, fetching documentation, or processing log files can consume significant context. By delegating these to a subagent, the verbose output stays in the subagent's context while only the relevant summary returns to your main conversation.
723	
724	```text theme={null}
725	Use a subagent to run the test suite and report only the failing tests with their error messages
726	```
727	
728	#### Run parallel research
729	
730	For independent investigations, spawn multiple subagents to work simultaneously:
731	
732	```text theme={null}
733	Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents
734	```
735	
736	Each subagent explores its area independently, then Claude synthesizes the findings. This works best when the research paths don't depend on each other.
737	
738	<Warning>
739	  When subagents complete, their results return to your main conversation. Running many subagents that each return detailed results can consume significant context.
740	</Warning>
741	
742	For tasks that need sustained parallelism or exceed your context window, [agent teams](/en/agent-teams) give each worker its own independent context.
743	
744	#### Chain subagents
745	
746	For multi-step workflows, ask Claude to use subagents in sequence. Each subagent completes its task and returns results to Claude, which then passes relevant context to the next subagent.
747	
748	```text theme={null}
749	Use the code-reviewer subagent to find performance issues, then use the optimizer subagent to fix them
750	```
751	
752	### Choose between subagents and main conversation
753	
754	Use the **main conversation** when:
755	
756	* The task needs frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement
757	* Multiple phases share significant context (planning → implementation → testing)
758	* You're making a quick, targeted change
759	* Latency matters. Subagents start fresh and may need time to gather context
760	
761	Use **subagents** when:
762	
763	* The task produces verbose output you don't need in your main context
764	* You want to enforce specific tool restrictions or permissions
765	* The work is self-contained and can return a summary
766	
767	Consider [Skills](/en/skills) instead when you want reusable prompts or workflows that run in the main conversation context rather than isolated subagent context.
768	
769	For a quick question about something already in your conversation, use [`/btw`](/en/interactive-mode#side-questions-with-%2Fbtw) instead of a subagent. It sees your full context but has no tool access, and the answer is discarded rather than added to history.
770	
771	<Note>
772	  Subagents cannot spawn other subagents. If your workflow requires nested delegation, use [Skills](/en/skills) or [chain subagents](#chain-subagents) from the main conversation.
773	</Note>
774	
775	### Manage subagent context
776	
777	#### What loads at startup
778	
779	Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It does not see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read. Claude composes a delegation message that summarizes the task, and the subagent works from there. The exception is a [fork](#fork-the-current-conversation), which inherits the parent conversation instead of starting fresh.
780	
781	A non-fork subagent's initial context contains:
782	
783	* **System prompt**: the agent's own prompt plus environment details that Claude Code appends, not the full Claude Code system prompt. Custom subagents define theirs in the [markdown body](#write-subagent-files) or `prompt` field. Built-in agents have predefined prompts.
784	* **Task message**: the delegation prompt Claude writes when it hands off the work.
785	* **CLAUDE.md and memory**: every level of the [memory hierarchy](/en/memory#how-claude-md-files-load) the main conversation loads, including `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, project rules, `CLAUDE.local.md`, and managed policy files. The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip this.
786	* **Git status**: a snapshot taken at the start of the parent session. Absent when the working directory isn't a Git repository or when [`includeGitInstructions`](/en/settings#available-settings) is `false`. Explore and Plan skip it regardless.
787	* **Preloaded skills**: full content of any skill named in the agent's [`skills` field](#preload-skills-into-subagents). Built-in agents don't preload skills.
788	
789	Explore and Plan are the only subagents that omit CLAUDE.md and git status. There is no frontmatter field or per-agent setting to change which agents skip them.
790	
791	The main conversation reads Explore and Plan results with full CLAUDE.md context, so most rules don't need to reach the subagent itself. If a rule must, such as "ignore the `vendor/` directory," restate it in the prompt you give Claude when delegating.
792	
793	#### Resume subagents
794	
795	Each subagent invocation creates a new instance with fresh context. To continue an existing subagent's work instead of starting over, ask Claude to resume it.
796	
797	Resumed subagents retain their full conversation history, including all previous tool calls, results, and reasoning. The subagent picks up exactly where it stopped rather than starting fresh.
798	
799	When a subagent completes, Claude receives its agent ID. The built-in Explore and Plan agents are one-shot and return no agent ID, so they can't be resumed; use `general-purpose` or a custom subagent when you need to continue the work. Claude uses the `SendMessage` tool with the agent's ID as the `to` field to resume it. The `SendMessage` tool is only available when [agent teams](/en/agent-teams) are enabled via `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`.
800	
801	To resume a subagent, ask Claude to continue the previous work:
802	
803	```text theme={null}
804	Use the code-reviewer subagent to review the authentication module
805	[Agent completes]
806	
807	Continue that code review and now analyze the authorization logic
808	[Claude resumes the subagent with full context from previous conversation]
809	```
810	
811	If a stopped subagent receives a `SendMessage`, it auto-resumes in the background without requiring a new `Agent` invocation.
812	
813	You can also ask Claude for the agent ID if you want to reference it explicitly, or find IDs in the transcript files at `~/.claude/projects/{project}/{sessionId}/subagents/`. Each transcript is stored as `agent-{agentId}.jsonl`.
814	
815	Subagent transcripts persist independently of the main conversation:
816	
817	* **Main conversation compaction**: When the main conversation compacts, subagent transcripts are unaffected. They're stored in separate files.
818	* **Session persistence**: Subagent transcripts persist within their session. You can [resume a subagent](#resume-subagents) after restarting Claude Code by resuming the same session.
819	* **Automatic cleanup**: Transcripts are cleaned up based on the `cleanupPeriodDays` setting (default: 30 days).
820	
821	#### Auto-compaction
822	
823	Subagents support automatic compaction using the same logic as the main conversation. By default, auto-compaction triggers at approximately 95% capacity. To trigger compaction earlier, set `CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE` to a lower percentage (for example, `50`). See [environment variables](/en/env-vars) for details.
824	
825	Compaction events are logged in subagent transcript files:
826	
827	```json theme={null}
828	{
829	  "type": "system",
830	  "subtype": "compact_boundary",
831	  "compactMetadata": {
832	    "trigger": "auto",
833	    "preTokens": 167189
834	  }
835	}
836	```
837	
838	The `preTokens` value shows how many tokens were used before compaction occurred.
839	
840	## Fork the current conversation
841	
842	<Note>
843	  Forked subagents require Claude Code v2.1.117 or later. {/* min-version: 2.1.161 */}From v2.1.161 the `/fork` command is enabled by default; on earlier versions it requires setting the [`CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT`](/en/env-vars) environment variable to `1`. Making forks the model's *default* spawn behavior is experimental and may change in future releases. This default may also be enabled in interactive sessions as part of a staged rollout.
844	</Note>
845	
846	A fork is a subagent that inherits the entire conversation so far instead of starting fresh. This drops the input isolation that subagents otherwise provide: a fork sees the same system prompt, tools, model, and message history as the main session, so you can hand it a side task without re-explaining the situation. The fork's own tool calls still stay out of your conversation and only its final result comes back, so your main context window stays clean. Use a fork when a named subagent would need too much background to be useful, or when you want to try several approaches in parallel from the same starting point.
847	
848	To control fork mode regardless of the staged rollout, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT`](/en/env-vars) to `1` to enable it explicitly or to `0` to disable it. The variable is honored in interactive mode and via the SDK or `claude -p`.
849	
850	Enabling fork mode changes Claude Code in two ways:
851	
852	* Claude spawns a fork whenever it would otherwise use the [general-purpose](#built-in-subagents) subagent. Named subagents such as Explore still spawn as before.
853	* Every subagent spawn runs in the [background](#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background), whether it is a fork or a named subagent. Set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS` to `1` to keep spawns synchronous.
854	
855	You can start a fork yourself with `/fork` followed by a directive, with or without the variable set. Claude Code names the fork from the first words of the directive. The following example forks the conversation to draft test cases while you continue with the implementation in the main session:
856	
857	```text theme={null}
858	/fork draft unit tests for the parser changes so far
859	```
860	
861	The fork appears in a panel below your prompt and runs in the background while you keep working. When it finishes, its result arrives as a message in your main conversation. The next section covers the panel controls for watching and steering forks while they run.
862	
863	### Observe and steer running forks
864	
865	Running forks appear in a panel below the prompt input, with one row for the main session and one for each fork. Use these keys to interact with the panel:
866	
867	| Key       | Action                                                             |
868	| :-------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------- |
869	| `↑` / `↓` | Move between rows                                                  |
870	| `Enter`   | Open the selected fork's transcript and send it follow-up messages |
871	| `x`       | Dismiss a finished fork or stop a running one                      |
872	| `Esc`     | Return focus to the prompt input                                   |
873	
874	### How forks differ from named subagents
875	
876	A fork inherits everything the main session has at the moment it spawns. A named subagent starts from its own definition.
877	
878	|                         | Fork                             | Named subagent                                                                           |
879	| :---------------------- | :------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
880	| Context                 | Full conversation history        | Fresh context with the prompt you pass                                                   |
881	| System prompt and tools | Same as main session             | From the subagent's [definition file](#write-subagent-files)                             |
882	| Model                   | Same as main session             | From the subagent's `model` field                                                        |
883	| Permissions             | Prompts surface in your terminal | [Auto-denied](#run-subagents-in-foreground-or-background) when running in the background |
884	| Prompt cache            | Shared with main session         | Separate cache                                                                           |
885	
886	Because a fork's system prompt and tool definitions are identical to the parent, its first request reuses the parent's [prompt cache](/en/prompt-caching#subagents-and-the-cache). This makes forking cheaper than spawning a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context.
887	
888	When Claude spawns a fork through the Agent tool, it can pass `isolation: "worktree"` so the fork's file edits are written to a separate git worktree instead of your checkout.
889	
890	### Limitations
891	
892	Setting `CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=1` enables fork mode in interactive sessions, [non-interactive mode](/en/headless), and the Agent SDK; setting it to `0` disables fork mode everywhere, including any server-side rollout. A fork cannot spawn further forks.
893	
894	## Example subagents
895	
896	These examples demonstrate effective patterns for building subagents. Use them as starting points, or generate a customized version with Claude.
897	
898	<Tip>
899	  **Best practices:**
900	
901	  * **Design focused subagents:** each subagent should excel at one specific task
902	  * **Write detailed descriptions:** Claude uses the description to decide when to delegate
903	  * **Limit tool access:** grant only necessary permissions for security and focus
904	  * **Check into version control:** share project subagents with your team
905	</Tip>
906	
907	### Code reviewer
908	
909	A read-only subagent that reviews code without modifying it. This example shows how to design a focused subagent with limited tool access (no Edit or Write) and a detailed prompt that specifies exactly what to look for and how to format output.
910	
911	```markdown theme={null}
912	---
913	name: code-reviewer
914	description: Expert code review specialist. Proactively reviews code for quality, security, and maintainability. Use immediately after writing or modifying code.
915	tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
916	model: inherit
917	---
918	
919	You are a senior code reviewer ensuring high standards of code quality and security.
920	
921	When invoked:
922	1. Run git diff to see recent changes
923	2. Focus on modified files
924	3. Begin review immediately
925	
926	Review checklist:
927	- Code is clear and readable
928	- Functions and variables are well-named
929	- No duplicated code
930	- Proper error handling
931	- No exposed secrets or API keys
932	- Input validation implemented
933	- Good test coverage
934	- Performance considerations addressed
935	
936	Provide feedback organized by priority:
937	- Critical issues (must fix)
938	- Warnings (should fix)
939	- Suggestions (consider improving)
940	
941	Include specific examples of how to fix issues.
942	```
943	
944	### Debugger
945	
946	A subagent that can both analyze and fix issues. Unlike the code reviewer, this one includes Edit because fixing bugs requires modifying code. The prompt provides a clear workflow from diagnosis to verification.
947	
948	```markdown theme={null}
949	---
950	name: debugger
951	description: Debugging specialist for errors, test failures, and unexpected behavior. Use proactively when encountering any issues.
952	tools: Read, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob
953	---
954	
955	You are an expert debugger specializing in root cause analysis.
956	
957	When invoked:
958	1. Capture error message and stack trace
959	2. Identify reproduction steps
960	3. Isolate the failure location
961	4. Implement minimal fix
962	5. Verify solution works
963	
964	Debugging process:
965	- Analyze error messages and logs
966	- Check recent code changes
967	- Form and test hypotheses
968	- Add strategic debug logging
969	- Inspect variable states
970	
971	For each issue, provide:
972	- Root cause explanation
973	- Evidence supporting the diagnosis
974	- Specific code fix
975	- Testing approach
976	- Prevention recommendations
977	
978	Focus on fixing the underlying issue, not the symptoms.
979	```
980	
981	### Data scientist
982	
983	A domain-specific subagent for data analysis work. This example shows how to create subagents for specialized workflows outside of typical coding tasks. It explicitly sets `model: sonnet` for more capable analysis.
984	
985	```markdown theme={null}
986	---
987	name: data-scientist
988	description: Data analysis expert for SQL queries, BigQuery operations, and data insights. Use proactively for data analysis tasks and queries.
989	tools: Bash, Read, Write
990	model: sonnet
991	---
992	
993	You are a data scientist specializing in SQL and BigQuery analysis.
994	
995	When invoked:
996	1. Understand the data analysis requirement
997	2. Write efficient SQL queries
998	3. Use BigQuery command line tools (bq) when appropriate
999	4. Analyze and summarize results
1000	5. Present findings clearly
1001	
1002	Key practices:
1003	- Write optimized SQL queries with proper filters
1004	- Use appropriate aggregations and joins
1005	- Include comments explaining complex logic
1006	- Format results for readability
1007	- Provide data-driven recommendations
1008	
1009	For each analysis:
1010	- Explain the query approach
1011	- Document any assumptions
1012	- Highlight key findings
1013	- Suggest next steps based on data
1014	
1015	Always ensure queries are efficient and cost-effective.
1016	```
1017	
1018	### Database query validator
1019	
1020	A subagent that allows Bash access but validates commands to permit only read-only SQL queries. This example shows how to use `PreToolUse` hooks for conditional validation when you need finer control than the `tools` field provides.
1021	
1022	```markdown theme={null}
1023	---
1024	name: db-reader
1025	description: Execute read-only database queries. Use when analyzing data or generating reports.
1026	tools: Bash
1027	hooks:
1028	  PreToolUse:
1029	    - matcher: "Bash"
1030	      hooks:
1031	        - type: command
1032	          command: "./scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh"
1033	---
1034	
1035	You are a database analyst with read-only access. Execute SELECT queries to answer questions about the data.
1036	
1037	When asked to analyze data:
1038	1. Identify which tables contain the relevant data
1039	2. Write efficient SELECT queries with appropriate filters
1040	3. Present results clearly with context
1041	
1042	You cannot modify data. If asked to INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or modify schema, explain that you only have read access.
1043	```
1044	
1045	Claude Code [passes hook input as JSON](/en/hooks#pretooluse-input) via stdin to hook commands. The validation script reads this JSON, extracts the command being executed, and checks it against a list of SQL write operations. If a write operation is detected, the script [exits with code 2](/en/hooks#exit-code-2-behavior-per-event) to block execution and returns an error message to Claude via stderr.
1046	
1047	Create the validation script anywhere in your project. The path must match the `command` field in your hook configuration:
1048	
1049	```bash theme={null}
1050	#!/bin/bash
1051	# Blocks SQL write operations, allows SELECT queries
1052	
1053	# Read JSON input from stdin
1054	INPUT=$(cat)
1055	
1056	# Extract the command field from tool_input using jq
1057	COMMAND=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.tool_input.command // empty')
1058	
1059	if [ -z "$COMMAND" ]; then
1060	  exit 0
1061	fi
1062	
1063	# Block write operations (case-insensitive)
1064	if echo "$COMMAND" | grep -iE '\b(INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|CREATE|ALTER|TRUNCATE|REPLACE|MERGE)\b' > /dev/null; then
1065	  echo "Blocked: Write operations not allowed. Use SELECT queries only." >&2
1066	  exit 2
1067	fi
1068	
1069	exit 0
1070	```
1071	
1072	On macOS and Linux, make the script executable:
1073	
1074	```bash theme={null}
1075	chmod +x ./scripts/validate-readonly-query.sh
1076	```
1077	
1078	On Windows, write the validation script in PowerShell and add `shell: powershell` to the hook entry. See [running hooks in PowerShell](/en/hooks#windows-powershell-tool).
1079	
1080	The hook receives JSON via stdin with the Bash command in `tool_input.command`. Exit code 2 blocks the operation and feeds the error message back to Claude. See [Hooks](/en/hooks#exit-code-output) for details on exit codes and [Hook input](/en/hooks#pretooluse-input) for the complete input schema.
